title: The paradox of macrorewilding and microdefaunation in post‐agrarian landscapes
content:
These contrasting biodiversity trends should be considered jointly when assessing conservation outcomes and ecosystem trajectories in post-agrarian landscapes. We highlight the need for multi-trophic monitoring, conservation success metrics that integrate different body sizes and trophic levels and coordinated approaches that address the management challenges associated with the recovery of large fauna while counteracting declines among small-bodied taxa.


Abstract

Disentangling biodiversity trends is a central challenge in ecological research. Here, we examine an overlooked paradox occurring across many post-agrarian landscape mosaics: while populations of several large-bodied animal taxa such as ungulates, carnivores and raptors are recovering (i.e., macrorewilding), many small-bodied vertebrate and invertebrate taxa including passerines, arthropods and amphibians are declining (i.e., microdefaunation). Although these opposing trends can emerge within the same broader post-agrarian transition, they have rarely been examined jointly. Land abandonment, reduced persecution and conservation policies have facilitated macrorewilding, whereas agricultural intensification and further drivers of global change contribute to microdefaunation through processes operating at different spatial scales. Macrorewilding often unfolds across broad regions, whereas microdefaunation may be expressed more heterogeneously at finer spatial grains for many taxa, producing uneven spatial overlap between the two processes. Where macrorewilding and microdefaunation co-occur, these opposing biodiversity trends may generate historically non-analogous community configurations through novel combinations of recovering large-bodied fauna and declining small-bodied taxa. Evidence from particular systems supports several trophic and non-trophic interactions between large- and small-bodied fauna, including predation, competition, ecosystem engineering and vegetation-mediated habitat change. We hypothesize that, within such emerging community configurations, recurrent and ecologically relevant interactions between both components may alter community functioning. Policy implications. These contrasting biodiversity trends should be considered jointly when assessing conservation outcomes and ecosystem trajectories in post-agrarian landscapes. We highlight the need for multi-trophic monitoring, conservation success metrics that integrate different body sizes and trophic levels and coordinated approaches that address the management challenges associated with the recovery of large fauna while counteracting declines among small-bodied taxa.
